analysis.one_liner: Bars big oil refiners from running their own gas stations and locking dealers into exclusive fuel purchases.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: introduced in September 1990, sent to a Senate Judiciary subcommittee in October, and it died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The Motor Fuel Consumer Protection Act would have rewritten the antitrust rules for the retail gasoline market. It would cap at 70% the share of their fuel that oil producers and refiners could force station dealers to buy from them, let dealers buy from wholesalers instead, and require a notice at the pump when fuel at a branded station did not come from that brand. Most strikingly, it would have made it illegal for any "large integrated refiner" — a company that both produces over 30% of its own crude and refines more than 175,000 barrels per day — to operate a gas station in the United States at all, forcing the oil majors out of direct retail and leaving stations in the hands of independent dealers.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers, who would face more competition at the wholesale and retail level, and independent gas station dealers and wholesalers, who could buy fuel from any wholesaler rather than being locked into their refiner's supply. Dealers also gained a private right to sue with attorney's fees paid by the losing refiner, and the Federal Trade Commission could have enforced the rules directly.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drivers and independent gas station dealers

how_it_helps.text: Caps at 70% of a dealer's monthly sales the share of fuel a producer or refiner could force a station to buy from it, and makes it illegal to stop a dealer from buying any or all of its fuel from a wholesaler — loosening the refiners' grip on who stations could buy from and at what price.

Makes it unlawful for any large integrated refiner — one that produces over 30% of the crude feeding its refineries and refines more than 175,000 barrels per day — to operate a gas station in the United States, pushing retail sales into the hands of independent dealers and franchisees.

Requires a clear notice at the pump when fuel sold at a station carrying a refiner's brand was not actually supplied by that refiner, so drivers know what they are buying; it also lets dealers convert or add tanks and dispensers to sell other suppliers' fuel.

Enforces the rules two ways: the Federal Trade Commission can sue violators in court for injunctions and monetary penalties, and any person affected can sue for damages and injunctive relief, with attorney and expert witness fees paid by the defendant if the plaintiff prevails.
Lets state consumer protections stand: the act would not supersede comparable state laws where both could be followed.

analysis.who_pays: Large integrated oil producers and refiners, which would lose the ability to require dealers to buy from them, to block wholesaler purchases, and to operate their own branded service stations. Some compliance and litigation costs could eventually be passed to consumers in the form of higher wholesale prices or fewer company-run stations.

drawbacks.text: Forcing refiners out of operating their own stations and capping supply contracts at 70% could disrupt existing retail networks and supply logistics, and refiners argued this era that company-run stations kept prices competitive — an honest supporter would concede the bill bet the retail market on independent dealers being more competitive than vertically integrated majors.

The private right of action with mandatory attorney's fees invites litigation between dealers and refiners over contract terms, and the FTC would have had to build new reporting regulations within 180 days, adding compliance costs that could be passed through at the pump.

The notice-at-the-pump rule for unbranded fuel at branded stations adds labeling requirements for small dealers, and the state-law savings clause creates a patchwork of overlapping state and federal rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits for consumers and independent dealers were real but indirect — more competition in wholesale fuel supply and an oil-majors-free retail market — and the bill carried genuine costs: disruption of established retail networks, litigation risk, and new regulatory machinery. It was a focused, fairly drawn proposal rather than a sweeping rewrite; its failure to move says more about its thin support in the Senate than about a flaw in its design.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee in September 1990, sent to its antitrust subcommittee a month later, and then sat there until the 101st Congress ended in January 1991 — no hearing, no markup, no vote on the floor.

narrative.text: Sen. Dennis DeConcini of Arizona, joined by Sen. Howard Metzenbaum of Ohio, introduced the bill on September 13, 1990, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day.
On October 23, 1990, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Antitrust, Monopolies and Business — the subcommittee covering antitrust policy — and no further action was ever taken on it.
Three Senate Democrats cosponsored the bill, and no further cosponsors were added before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, leaving the bill to die without a committee vote or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large integrated oil refiners, who kept the ability to operate their own service stations and require dealers to buy from them, and the congressional leaders who never had to take a position, since the bill died quietly in committee.

for.name: Dennis DeConcini
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited its three cosponsors.

for.name: Howard Metzenbaum
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only original co-sponsor at introduction.

for.name: 3 of 55 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no additional members signed on before it died.

against.name: Joseph Biden
against.what_they_did: The committee the bill was referred to never took it up — no hearing or markup appears in the record between the September 1990 referral and the end of the Congress.

against.name: Large integrated oil refiners
against.what_they_did: The bill targeted the major oil companies' control of retail gasoline, and the industry opposed divorcement and open-supply legislation of this kind during this period.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so the partisan split never got tested; all known supporters, including the sponsor, the sole original co-sponsor, and the three cosponsors, were Democrats.

industries.industry: Large integrated oil refiners (Exxon, Shell, Texaco and similar majors)
industries.note: The bill would have made it illegal for them to operate their own gas stations and would have capped at 70% the share of fuel they could require dealers to buy from them, dismantling the vertical control the majors had built over retail gasoline. Its death left their retail networks and supply lock-in intact.

Refiners would no longer be able to restrain dealers from buying from wholesalers of the refiner's own brand fuel, opening a bigger wholesale market. The bill died before any of this could take effect.

industries.industry: Gasoline service station dealers and franchisees
industries.note: Dealers would have gained freedom to source fuel, the right to add tanks for other suppliers at branded stations, and a private right of action with attorney's fees against refiners who violated the rules.
